title: Song of Solomon 4:1–16
context: A single poem of praise and invitation. In the WEB speaker headings, the Lover speaks 4:1–15, praising the beloved with images from the countryside and calling her a locked garden and a sealed fountain, and the Beloved answers in 4:16, inviting him into the garden. Readers in both traditions have read the Song literally, as a celebration of covenant love between husband and wife, and allegorically, as a picture of God and Israel or Christ and the church; neither approach is treated here as the only faithful one. Speaker headings are editorial aids, not part of the original text.

verses.text: Behold, you are beautiful, my love. Behold, you are beautiful. Your eyes are like doves behind your veil. Your hair is as a flock of goats, that descend from Mount Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: In the WEB headings the Lover speaks: “Behold, you are beautiful, my love.” Arminian readers who take the Song literally see delight and honor within covenant love; those who read allegorically hear Christ’s regard for his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold both approaches. Some read the praise as celebrating faithful married love as God’s good gift, while others, following a long Christian practice, hear Christ’s love for the church. The poem’s imagery is drawn from the countryside, such as doves and flocks.

verses.text: Your teeth are like a newly shorn flock, which have come up from the washing, where every one of them has twins. None is bereaved among them.
verses.arminianNotes: The praise continues with pastoral images of a shorn flock and twins. Arminian readers see the poet using familiar rural pictures to express wholeness and freshness, without needing to press each detail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see figurative language meant to convey beauty and completeness. Readers in this tradition commonly caution against forcing a symbolic meaning onto every image, whichever reading of the Song they adopt.

verses.text: Your lips are like scarlet thread. Your mouth is lovely. Your temples are like a piece of a pomegranate behind your veil.
verses.arminianNotes: Scarlet thread and pomegranate are used as images of loveliness. Arminian readers see poetry that honors the beloved with images of color and fruitfulness familiar to its first hearers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see vivid, respectful imagery. Allegorical readers have sometimes drawn spiritual lessons from these details, while literal readers stress the dignity of the person praised; both approaches appear within this tradition.

verses.text: Your neck is like David’s tower built for an armory, on which a thousand shields hang, all the shields of the mighty men.
verses.arminianNotes: The beloved’s neck is compared to “David’s tower built for an armory,” hung with shields. Arminian readers see an image of dignity and strength rather than mere prettiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a picture of noble bearing. The tower is not identified elsewhere in Scripture, and readers in this tradition hold any identification of it, or of its symbolism, with caution.

verses.text: Your two breasts are like two fawns that are twins of a roe, which feed among the lilies.
verses.arminianNotes: The praise uses images of twin fawns feeding among the lilies. Arminian readers see gentle, pastoral language that expresses tender delight while remaining restrained and modest in its imagery.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the poet drawing on nature to express affection. Readers in this tradition stress reading such lines soberly, whether they understand the Song as human love or as a picture of Christ and his people.

verses.text: Until the day is cool, and the shadows flee away, I will go to the mountain of myrrh, to the hill of frankincense.
verses.arminianNotes: “Until the day is cool, and the shadows flee away, I will go to the mountain of myrrh.” Arminian readers see longing and resolve expressed through images of fragrance and evening.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a poetic expression of devotion. Allegorical readers have often linked myrrh and frankincense with worship, while literal readers see the language of courtship; the text does not settle the matter.

verses.text: You are all beautiful, my love. There is no spot in you.
verses.arminianNotes: “You are all beautiful, my love. There is no spot in you.” Arminian readers who read allegorically often connect this with Christ presenting the church without spot, as in Ephesians 5:27.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that allegorical readers make that connection, while literal readers hear a lover’s wholehearted admiration. Readers in this tradition hold both approaches without making either a test of faithfulness.

verses.text: Come with me from Lebanon, my bride, with me from Lebanon. Look from the top of Amana, from the top of Senir and Hermon, from the lions’ dens, from the mountains of the leopards.
verses.arminianNotes: “Come with me from Lebanon, my bride,” from Amana, Senir, Hermon, and the lairs of lions and leopards. Arminian readers see an invitation to leave danger and distance for the lover’s company.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a call away from remote and dangerous places. Senir is linked with Hermon in Deuteronomy 3:9, though readers in this tradition hold the precise geography of Amana with some caution.

verses.text: You have ravished my heart, my sister, my bride. You have ravished my heart with one of your eyes, with one chain of your neck.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have ravished my heart, my sister, my bride.” Arminian readers see the deep effect of love, expressed with the affectionate titles of family and covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see language of covenant closeness, since “sister” and “bride” express intimacy and belonging. Allegorical readers apply it to God’s love for his people; literal readers to marriage.

verses.text: How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride! How much better is your love than wine, the fragrance of your perfumes than all kinds of spices!
verses.arminianNotes: “How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride! How much better is your love than wine.” Arminian readers see love valued above ordinary pleasures, echoing praise heard earlier in the Song.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see love prized above delights such as wine and spices. The comparison recalls 1:2, and readers in this tradition note how the Song repeats and develops its themes.

verses.text: Your lips, my bride, drip like the honeycomb. Honey and milk are under your tongue. The smell of your garments is like the smell of Lebanon.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your lips, my bride, drip like the honeycomb. Honey and milk are under your tongue.” Arminian readers see sweetness of speech and character praised in images of abundance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see images of richness and delight. Some readers hear an echo of the land flowing with milk and honey (Exodus 3:8), though this connection is suggested rather than stated in the text.

verses.text: My sister, my bride, is a locked up garden; a locked up spring, a sealed fountain.
verses.arminianNotes: “My sister, my bride, is a locked up garden; a locked up spring, a sealed fountain.” Arminian readers see faithfulness and exclusive devotion pictured in protected, reserved places.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see images of purity and belonging. Allegorical readers apply the enclosed garden to God’s people set apart for him, while literal readers see the faithfulness of married love.

verses.text: Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates, with precious fruits, henna with spikenard plants,
verses.arminianNotes: “Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates, with precious fruits, henna with spikenard plants.” Arminian readers see the garden image expanded to express fruitfulness and value.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see abundance pictured in a well-tended garden. The exact identification of some plants named here is uncertain, and readers in this tradition do not press them.

verses.text: spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with every kind of incense tree; myrrh and aloes, with all the best spices,
verses.arminianNotes: The list continues with spikenard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, incense trees, myrrh, and aloes. Arminian readers see a profusion of fragrances expressing the rich worth of the one praised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a catalog of precious spices conveying delight. Several of these plants are difficult to identify with certainty, and readers in this tradition treat the list as poetic rather than botanical.

verses.text: a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing streams from Lebanon.
verses.arminianNotes: “… a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing streams from Lebanon.” Arminian readers see refreshment and life pictured in flowing water.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see images of vitality. Allegorical readers sometimes compare the living waters with passages such as John 4:10, though literal readers see a lover’s praise; both approaches are held within this tradition.

verses.text: Awake, north wind, and come, you south! Blow on my garden, that its spices may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and taste his precious fruits.
verses.arminianNotes: The WEB heading marks the Beloved: “Awake, north wind, and come, you south! … Let my beloved come into his garden.” Arminian readers see mutual love freely welcomed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the beloved responding to the lover’s praise with an invitation. The garden image now becomes hers to offer, expressing reciprocity, whether read as human love or as the church welcoming Christ.
